newsitem.title: UK: SOCCER SHOWCASE-CHELSEA CAPTURE MOOD OF MOMENT 27 YEARS ON.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER SHOWCASE-CHELSEA CAPTURE MOOD OF MOMENT 27 YEARS ON.

text.p: They may no longer sport kipper ties and bushy sideburns, but todays Chelsea F.A. Cup winners represent football chic in the 90s every bit as much as their counterparts did in 1970.

The southwest London club last won the Cup 27 years ago, when the King's Road was still at the heart of swinging London, Harold Wilson was Prime Minister and the Beatles were fighting over Yoko and Apple.
In 1997, London is once again the cool captial, the King's Road hums to the strains of myriad musical styles from Spice Girls to Jungle and the trendy restaurants are modern Italian.
Ruud Gullit's eclectic band of foreign and cockney talent, dominated by Italian style, has captured the mood of the moment.

And though Saturday's 2-0 win over Middlesbrough may not entirely have lived up to its entertainment billing, Roberto Di Matteo's stunning individual goal just 42.4 seconds into the match was a fitting piece of Italian flamboyance.
There are parallels between the two Cup winning sides.
Chelsea lifted the 1970 trophy three years after losing the final to Tottenham. In 1994 the club was beaten at Wembley by Manchester United.
Like the modern Chelsea side, the 1969-70 team were considered one of the most fashionable and entertaining if inconsistent teams in the league.

They enjoyed a wealth of individual talent such as that of agile goal keeper Peter Bonetti, Scottish international Charlie Cooke, who would run rings round the opposition in midfield, and Peter Osgood, still the last man to score in every round of the Cup.

Today diminutive striker Gianfranco Zola, dubbed "happy feet" by captain Dennis Wise, has captivated the premier league with his ball skills, Mark Hughes, a long-time Manchester United striker has found a new lease of life down south and Gianluca Vialli is the sort of subsititute other teams dream of.
And there the differences begin. Vialli, who lifted the European Cup as Captain of Juventus a year ago, earns more in a week than most Englishmen in a year and he spends a lot of time on the bench.
In 1970 top players were comfortable, but they were hardly millionaires and none of them came from Italy.
The team that walked out on to Wembley turf last Saturday contained only four English players, alongside two Italians a Romanian, a Norwegian, a Frenchman a Scot and Welsh international Hughes.
It also had two homegrown black players -- unknown to Stamford Bridge in 1970 --and a dreadlocked manager whose father comes from Surinam and mother from the Netherlands.
The 1970 side considered themselves exotic with three Scotsman, an Irish defender and a goalkeeper whose grandparents came from Switzerland.
Coaching styles are also worlds apart. Dave Sexton was of the old school of autocratic management, who tried to keep his players away from the seductive pleasures of the King's Road and West End.
Gullit, the first foreign coach to reach a Cup final, is a much more relaxed character. "What the players do in their own time is their own business," he said recently. "I want a happy squad."
Where Sexton was a dour character who fought shy of the limelight, Gullit is a gregarious, multilingual and highly articulate.

Unlike Sexton in 1970, Gullit is still a player and one who commands immense respect for his footballing achievements in winning the European championship as captain of the Netherlands and European Cup with AC Milan.
"He treats us like adults. He never raises his voice," said Steve Clarke, Chelsea's longest-serving first team player with 10 years at Stamford Bridge. "He knows what he wants and gets it."

Gullit admitted on Saturday that as an import he had not fully appreciated what it meant to Chelsea fans, whose teams have promised so much and produced so little over the past three decades, to bring the trophy home again.

He may have got an inkling on Sunday when upwards of 60,000 thronged the streets of to watch their heroes parade the Cup from Sloane Square to Fulham town hall, just as they had in 1970. Some things don't change.
